steps.title: Before: the nightly job everyone is afraid of
steps.plain: Every night this job rebuilds the gold revenue table from all 2 million orders (90 days). It takes 26.5 s on this laptop; the same shape of job on a real lake is the one that takes three hours. Four problems hide in it at once: the orders sit in 3,000 tiny files, a Python function labels every row, 40% of orders belong to one customer (guest checkout), and it rebuilds all 90 days to add one. Each step from here removes one problem and measures what it was worth.
steps.code:
orders = spark.table('orders')                      # 3,000 tiny files
orders = orders.withColumn('segment', segment_udf('amount'))   # Python UDF
gold = (orders.join(customers, 'customer_id')        # 40% of rows: customer 0
          .groupBy('order_date', 'segment', 'tier').agg(sum('amount'), count('*')))
gold.write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable('gold')     # all 90 days, every night

steps.plain: OPTIMIZE rewrote 3,000 tiny files into 1, sorted by order_date (ZORDER), so each file now covers a narrow range of days. Fewer files means fewer tasks to schedule and fewer files to open. 15.8 s → 2.2 s. The sort by date also pays off in fix 4.

steps.title: Fix 3: let adaptive execution split the hot customer
steps.plain: With adaptive query execution (AQE) on, Spark measures the shuffle after the first stage, sees one partition (customer 0) far bigger than the rest and splits it across several tasks. 2.2 s → 2.5 s: on two cores, splitting adds tasks without adding cores to run them, so here it did not help. On a cluster, where the slowest task sets the finish time, this is the fix that matters most (story 4 measures the critical path). Compare the slowest bars in the stages panel.

spark.conf.set('spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled', 'true')
# laptop scale: skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes = 1MB

steps.title: Fix 4: build only the day that changed
steps.plain: Tonight only 2026-09-28 has new orders, so the job reads that day (Delta skips the files whose date range cannot match, thanks to the ZORDER in fix 2) and replaces only that day in gold. 2.5 s → 2.2 s. Overall: 26.5 s → 2.2 s, about 11× faster, with the same answer. On a real lake this is the 3 hours to 5 minutes story. Here it is measured at laptop scale, and the waterfall shows what each fix was worth.

(job(day='2026-09-28')                                # read one day
   .write.mode('overwrite')
   .option('replaceWhere', "order_date = '2026-09-28'")    # replace one day
   .saveAsTable('gold'))

steps.title: Before: a join that multiplies rows
steps.plain: 500,000 orders joined to the product dimension. The dimension keeps history (SCD Type 2): 20 versions of every product. Joining on product_id alone matches every version, so each order becomes 20 rows: 10,000,000 rows came out of the join, and revenue is 20 times too high. 1.4 s. In production this is the job that never finishes, or finishes with a number nobody believes.

steps.title: Before: a small MERGE rewrites the whole table
steps.plain: Every day about 2,000 recent orders change. The MERGE matches them by order_id only. The table is not organised by date, so the changed rows are spread across all 16 files, and Delta rewrites every file that holds a matched row: 16 of 16 files rewritten, copying 1,998,000 unchanged rows to update 2,000. 2.5 s.
steps.code:
MERGE INTO orders t USING changes s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET amount = s.amount

steps.title: After: organise by date, and say so in the MERGE
steps.plain: The same table partitioned by month, and the MERGE condition names the month (all changes are recent). Delta now only looks at, and rewrites, files in that partition: 2 of 66 files, copying 50,000 rows to update 2,000. 2.5 s → 862 ms. Liquid clustering or ZORDER by date does the same for unpartitioned tables, and deletion vectors avoid rewriting files at all.

MERGE INTO orders t USING changes s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id AND t.month = '2026-09'   -- lets Delta skip every other month
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET amount = s.amount

steps.title: Before: one partition, and it does not fit in memory
steps.plain: Sorting 2.5 million wide rows (about 200 bytes each) with shuffle partitions set to 1, the way a config copied from a tiny test job might leave it. One task must sort everything; its data does not fit in the memory Spark gives it (this laptop's executor has 1 GB), so it writes sorted runs to disk and merges them back: spill. 7.5 s. Recorded spill: 128 MB written to disk.

wide.orderBy('h').write.format('noop').save()

steps.title: After: enough partitions that each slice fits in memory
steps.plain: With 32 shuffle partitions each task sorts about 15 MB, which fits in memory: no spill. 7.5 s → 6.2 s. This laptop's fast SSD makes spilling cheap, so the time gain here is modest; on cluster disks, with gigabytes per task, spill is often the difference between minutes and hours. A trap we hit while recording: with adaptive execution's partition coalescing on, Spark merged the 32 small partitions back into a few large ones (it aims for 64 MB each by default) and the spill came back. Set the shuffle partitions and AQE's target size together.
steps.code:
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', 32)
wide.orderBy('h').write.format('noop').save()

steps.title: Before: collect() pulls everything into the driver
steps.plain: To build a report, someone calls collect() on 3 million rows, bringing every row into the driver's memory. Here the driver's result limit (spark.driver.maxResultSize, set to 16 MB on this laptop) stopped it after 295 ms: Total size of serialized results of 1 tasks (19.3 MiB) is bigger than spark.driver.maxResultSize (16.0 MiB). Without that limit, the driver runs out of memory and the whole application dies, often hours into a job.

steps.title: After: partition by date (coarse), cluster by customer
steps.plain: Partition by month (9 folders), then OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY customer_id so each file holds a narrow range of customers. 9 files. Write plus OPTIMIZE: 2.6 s (was 24.0 s). The monthly report: 3.1 s → 212 ms. A one-customer query still skips most files using the per-file statistics (158 ms). Rule of thumb: partition only by a low-cardinality column you filter on, with partitions of about 1 GB or more; cluster by the rest.

steps.title: Before: the cluster that ran all weekend (illustrative)
steps.plain: Illustrative arithmetic, not a recording. An all-purpose cluster with 4 nodes was started on Friday at 18:00 to debug a job and never stopped. Its autoscaling minimum was 4, so it never shrank. Monday 09:00 is 63 hours later: 4 nodes × 63 h × 1.0 DBU = 252 DBU, at an example $0.55/DBU = $139, for a weekend with no new data. Rates here are examples; use your own price list.

cost = nodes × hours × DBU per node-hour × $ per DBU
     = 4 × 63 × 1.0 × 0.55 = $139

steps.title: After: job clusters, auto-termination, a budget alert (illustrative)
steps.plain: Scheduled work runs on job clusters (or serverless) that start for the job and stop after it, billed at the lower jobs rate (example $0.2/DBU). Interactive clusters get auto-termination after 15 minutes idle. A budget alert fires when spend passes a threshold. Same three nights of work: 4 × (6 h + 3 × 15 min) × 1.0 DBU × $0.2 = $5 instead of $139. Illustrative: the shape of the saving is typical; your numbers depend on your rates and cluster sizes.
